newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Boeing defends McDonnell merger at EU hearing.
newsitem.headline: Boeing defends McDonnell merger at EU hearing.

text.p: Boeing Co. executives met with EU officials and aviation industry counterparts Thursday armed with boxes of documents to defend their merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp. against charges of unfair competition.

Boeing's presentation marked the first day of a two-day, closed-door hearing organised by the European Commission, the EU's competition watchdog, to allow the U.S. manufacturer and its competitors to air their views about the takeover.

Boeing representatives, including the executive vice president of the commercial airplane group, Dick Albrecht, and the head of the merger transition team, Jerry King, declined to make any comment as they emerged for lunch. Others were equally tight-lipped.

The commission started a full probe into the $14 billion merger in March, worried that Boeing, which already controls 60 percent of the world market for commercial jet aircraft, will reinforce its position to an extent that could harm fair competition in the 15-nation European Union.
In the United States, Boeing and McDonnell Douglas have triggered a 20-day countdown to a government decision on their proposed $14 billion merger, a Boeing spokesman said Thursday.

The companies certified Wednesday that they have filed millions of pages of documents sought by the Federal Trade Commission to evaluate whether the merger meets requirements of the nation's antitrust laws.
The five-member FTC has until July 1 to make its decision. However, the countdown can be stopped at any time by mutual consent of the parties.

The timing in this case is important because Boeing and McDonnell Douglas want the American competition agency to rule before the European Union decides whether to approve the merger. Boeing and others have operated on the assumption that the Americans are likely to be more favourable to the merger than the European Union.

The Brussels hearing, which is being attended by Boeing's only serious rival, European consortium Airbus Industrie, is part of the EU's merger control procedure to help the commission reach its final decision due by July 31.
The two-day meeting is not due to produce any decisions or official statements.
Boeing has replied to the commission's objections, detailed in a 40-page dossier May 21, with a stack of documents about four inches thick, according to the source.
Evidence supplied to the hearing by the Seattle-based company appeared even weightier, with Boeing officials arriving laden down by several heavy boxes.

Friday will see the turn of Airbus's managing director, Jean Pierson; the consortium's partners and other interested parties to provide evidence on the implications of the merger, Airbus and other sources said.
Pierson said earlier this year that in the long term the merger would "pose a problem for Europe's civil aviation industry" but thought it was inevitable.

Daimler-Benz Aerospace and British Aerospace, which together with France's Aerospatiale and Construcciones Aeronauticas of Spain control Airbus, have been the most active in opposing Boeing's plans and in pushing for the transformation of Airbus into an independent company.
Lockheed Martin Co. was also expected to be represented at the meeting.
Boeing has rejected commission charges that its deal will damage competition, saying McDonnell Douglas's market share of new commercial jet sales is only 4 percent.
But there are many McDonnell Douglas aircraft in European airline fleets for which the commission believes Boeings will be the "natural" replacements.

According to Association of European Airlines figures, of the passenger jet aircraft flown by association members last year, 47 percent were Boeings, 22 percent McDonnell Douglas, 20 percent Airbus and 11 percent other manufacturers.
Figures for aircraft on order looked better for Airbus, which held 43 percent of the 301 aircraft on order compared with Boeing's 45 percent.
